'''Annie Leuch-Reineck''' (born '''Annie Reineck''': 26 November 1880 - 21 December 1978) was a Swiss mathematician and women's rights activist.   She was one of the most influential participants in the [[:de:Schweizer Frauenbewegung#1920er Jahre|Swiss women's movement]] during the 1920s and 1930s.<ref name=ALRlautRL>{{cite web|title=Leuch [-Reineck], Annie|date=16 January 2008|author=Regula Ludi|url=http://www.hls-dhs-dss.ch/textes/d/D9346.php| publisher=Historischen Lexikon der Schweiz, Bern|accessdate=3 August 2018}}</ref><ref name=ALRselonLRT>{{cite web|title=En mémoire d'Annie Leuch-Reineck ou Madame Annie Leuch|author=Lotti Ruckstuhl-Thalmessinger| publisher=Femmes suisses et le Mouvement féministe : organe officiel des informations de l'Alliance de Sociétés Féminines Suisses|work=Nouvelles de Suisse| volume=67 / 3|date=March 1979}}</ref>

== Life ==
=== Provenance and early years ===
Annie Reineck was born in [[Kannawurf]], a village in the countryside between [[Erfurt]] and [[Magdeburg]] in [[German empire|Germany]].   Erhard Reineck (1841–1932), her father, was a protestant [[Parson|church minister]] and [[Superintendent (ecclesiastical)|superintentant (church administrator)]] originally from [[Magdeburg]].   Her mother, born Marie Godet (1847–1936), was from [[Neuchâtel]] in [[Suisse Romande|francophone western]] [[Switzerland]].    Annie grew up in [[Kannawurf]] and then in nearby [[Heldrungen]].   She received her early education at the home of her elder sister, Theodora (Theodora Reineck, 1874–1963).   Later, between 1895 and 1898, she attended the "École Vinet", a secondary school in [[Lausanne]].<ref name=ALRlautRL/><ref name="Bastian2017">{{cite book|author=Jean-Pierre Bastian|title=La fracture religieuse vaudoise, 1847-1966: L'Eglise libre, "la Môme" et la canton de Vaud|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=mHU7DwAAQBAJ&pg=PT225|date=2 November 2017|publisher=Labor et Fides| isbn=978-2-8309-5077-9|pages=225–226}}</ref>   The school was headed up by her aunt, Sophie Godet.<ref>Silke Redolfi: Frauen bauen Staat, 100 Jahre Bund Schweizerischer Frauenorganisationen, NZZ-Verlag Zürich, 2000, p. 70, {{ISBN|3-85823-819-8}}</ref><ref name=EcoleVinet>{{cite web|url=http://www.davel.vd.ch/detail.aspx?ID=32460|publisher= Archives cantonales vaudoises|title=P Vinet (Ecole) Volée 1900 de l'Ecole Vinet, 1900.10.12-1968.09.13 (Fonds)|accessdate=3 August 2018}}</ref>

=== Student ===
Reineck enrolled at the [[University of Bern]] in 1901 or 1902.   She studied Mathematics and various Natural Sciences, notably Physics and Earth Sciences.   In 1905 she received a secondary school teaching certificate.<ref name=ALRlautRL/>   There were still very few female students at the university, and several of the members of the small "Bern Female Students' Association" (''"Berner Studentinnenverein"'') became, in different ways, pioneering feminists and lifelong friends.   For Annie Reineck these included [[Gertrud Woker]] (1878 - 1968) and the physician [[Ida Hoff]] (1880 - 1952).<ref name=IHlautFR>{{cite web|url=http://www.bezg.ch/img/publikation/02_3/rogger.pdf|title=Kropfkampagne, Malzbonbons und Frauenrechte ... Zum 50. Todestag der ersten Berner Schulärztin Dr. med. Ida Hoff, 1880–1952|work=Berner Zeitschrift für Geschichte| volume=01/17|author=Franziska Rogger|pages=105–106|accessdate=3 August 2018}}</ref>

=== Teacher ===
In 1907 Annie Reineck became the first German-language woman at the [[University of Bern]] to receive a doctorate in Mathematics.   Her dissertation concerned "The relationship between [[Spherical harmonics|spherical functions]] and [[Bessel function]]s" (''"Die Verwandtschaft zwischen Kugelfunktionen und Besselschen Funktionen"'').<ref name="Reineck1907">{{cite book|author=Annie Reineck|title=Die Verwandtschaft zwischen Kugelfunktionen und Besselschen Funktionen|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=bzsVAQAAIAAJ|year=1907|publisher=Universitat Bern.}}</ref>   From this point till 1925 she taught at the Girls' Secondary School in [[Bern]] (where [[Ida Hoff]] was appointed school doctor in 1913) and at the city's training college for women teachers.<ref name=ALRselonCDR>{{cite web|pages=8–9|title=Doktorandinnen in der Schweiz|url=http://www.europeanwomeninmaths.org/sites/default/files/documents/reports/frauenmathch.pdf|work=Wege von Frauen: Mathematikerinnen in der Schweiz|author=Christine Riedtmann|publisher=European Women in Mathematics|access-date=3 August 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170111082223/http://www.europeanwomeninmaths.org/sites/default/files/documents/reports/frauenmathch.pdf|archive-date=11 January 2017|url-status=dead|author-link=Christine Riedtmann}}</ref>

In 1913 she married the commercial lawyer Georg Leuch (1888 - 1959).   He became a [[Canton of Bern|cantonal]] high court judge in 1920 and a [[Federal Supreme Court of Switzerland|Federal Supreme Court]] Judge in 1925, which involved relocating to [[Lausanne]].<ref name=GLlautCZ>{{cite web|title=Leuch, Georg|date=16 September 2008|author=Christoph Zürcher| url=http://www.hls-dhs-dss.ch/textes/d/D43794.php| publisher=Historischen Lexikon der Schweiz, Bern|accessdate=3 August 2018}}</ref>   By this time Annie Leuch-Reineck's time and energies had become divided between mathematics teaching and political campaigning:  she now resigned from her teaching jobs in [[Bern]].<ref name=ALRlautRL/>

=== Women's rights ===
In 1916 she took on the leadership of the [[Bern]] section of the [[:de:Schweizerischer Verband für Frauenstimmrecht|"Swiss Association for Women's Voting Rights" (''"Schweizerischer Verband für Frauenstimmrecht"'')]].  In 1919 or 1921 she was a co-founder of the "Bernese Women's League" (''"Berner Frauenbund"'').<ref name=ALRlautRL/>  Between 1920 and 1933 she campaigned for the rights of Swiss women o retain their Swiss citizenship rights if they married a foreigner.   She was a member of various legal commissions established by the [[Alliance F|League of Swiss Women's Associations (''"Bund Schweizerischer Frauenvereine"'')]].  In 1921 she co-organised the "Second Swiss Congress for Women's Interests" (''"2. Schweizer Kongresses für Fraueninteressen"''), held that year in [[Bern]].   In 1928 she was appointed to the national presidency of the [[:de:Schweizerischer Verband für Frauenstimmrecht|"Swiss Association for Women's Voting Rights" (''"Schweizerischer Verband für Frauenstimmrecht"'')]], a post she retained till 1940.<ref name=ALRlautRL/>

She was also, from 1928, one of those working on the 1929 "Swiss Exhibition for Women's Work" (''"Schweizer Ausstellung für Frauenarbeit"'' / SAFFA).   In 1929 she led that year's petition demanding for women the right to vote.<ref name=Stimmrechtspetition>{{cite book| pages=9–16| title="Frauen scheren sich nicht um Politik" Wie Geschichte und Gegenwart Frauen aus der Politik rausdefinieren | author=Regula Stämpfli| volume=-25/26| date=2007| url=http://frauenarchivostschweiz.ch/files/olympe/olympe_25_26.pdf| isbn= 978-3-905087-48-2| work=Olympe: Feministische Arbeitshefte zur Politik| publisher=Olympe | accessdate=4 August 2018}}</ref>   She was a member of the national executive (''"Vorstand"'') of the "Swiss Social Policy Union" (''"Schweizer Vereinigung für Sozialpolitik"'') and a member of the commission set up by the [[International Alliance of Women|Weltbund für Frauenstimmrecht (''"International Alliance of Women"'')]] to enquire into the citizenship rights of wives.

== Family ==
Annie Leuch-Reineck was a grand daughter of the [[Continental Reformed church|reformist theologian]] Frédéric Louis Godet (1812–1900) from [[Neuchâtel]].

Her sister, Eva Reineck, was a professional violinist who built her career in [[Frankfurt am Main]] and married a graphic artist of Jewish provenance called David Spear.   Annie Leuch-Reineck was thereby an aunt to this couple's son, [[Walter Eric Spear]], a notable physicist who built his career in England and Scotland after the family managed to escape from Nazi Germany in 1938.
